A PLAYABLE THOUGHT EXPERIMENT 01 / COHERENCE

Can you tell two
quantum states apart?

This is a simulation of two ways to prepare four quantum bits. Each measurement gives a four-digit result, such as 0000 or 1111. The first measurement setting gives both preparations the same probabilities. Your task is to find a measurement that tells them apart.

Two preparations. One question.

01 — THE IDEA

The difference is in
how possibilities combine.

A mixture is an either/or.

Imagine a coin choosing between 0000 and 1111 before each trial. Each choice is definite. You just don’t know which one was picked.

A superposition carries phase.

The two possibilities are part of one quantum state. Their relative phase makes them reinforce or cancel when you measure in a different basis.

↳

For this superposition, the X view only produces outcomes with an odd number of 1s. The mixture produces odd and even outcomes equally often in the long run. Same first picture. Different underlying structure.

A small sample can be misleading. Seeing only odd outcomes is evidence within this two-choice game, not general proof of entanglement. Try fewer trials, then compare with the exact probabilities.

02 — WHY I BUILT THIS

Why I came back
to this circuit.

I was a quantum mechanics fanatic as a kid. At Brown, I got to explore it through quantum mechanics and computational physics coursework. Now I want to turn that curiosity into something you can play.

This starts with a four-qubit circuit I studied, and a simple question: what can a measurement hide? You don’t need the maths to try the game. If you want it, the machinery is open below.

Dhiraj Khanal Physics, agents & experiments

Under the hoodThe states, the maths, and the limits ＋

The two preparations

Coherent: |GHZ−⟩ = (|0000⟩ − |1111⟩) / √2.

Mixture: ρ = ½|0000⟩⟨0000| + ½|1111⟩⟨1111|.

The Z view measures directly. The X view applies a Hadamard to each qubit before Z measurement. In this view, bit 0 records the +1 X outcome and bit 1 records −1. The minus sign in GHZ− determines the odd-parity result.

For the mixture, the chance of N independent X trials all having odd parity is 2−N. This is a likelihood under a specified model, not a posterior probability that your guess is right.

What is—and isn’t—being claimed

Established quantum mechanics, presented as an interactive experiment. No claim of a new algorithm or research result. The model assumes perfect preparation and measurement; there is no device noise.

The game promises exactly these two candidate preparations. It does not certify an arbitrary unknown state or a real device.

Bit strings display q4 q3 q2 q1. The browser samples the exact distributions; Python provides the independently tested reference.
